lines.text: Settled by ocean voyagers, ruled in turn by Germany and New Zealand, and the first Pacific nation to win back its freedom. This is the story of Samoa.
Some three thousand years ago, the Lapita people, makers of decorated pottery, sailed east and settled these islands.
From here their descendants crossed vast stretches of ocean by the stars and swells, and Samoa became a heart of Polynesia.
By the middle of the nineteenth century Apia, on the island of Upolu, had grown into a busy harbour town and the future capital.
The Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island, would spend his last years here.
In 1900 Germany took the western islands as a colony.
New Zealand seized them in 1914, and four years later the influenza pandemic arrived by ship, with terrible loss of life.
In 1957 Fiame Naomi Mata'afa was born. She would become Samoa's first woman prime minister.
In 1962, after years of the Mau movement for self-rule, Samoa became independent, the first Pacific island nation to do so.
Dwayne Johnson, born in 1972, would carry his Samoan heritage into the wrestling ring and onto movie screens worldwide.
And at the end of 2011, Samoa jumped across the date line, skipping the thirtieth of December entirely.
From canoe voyagers to a nation that moved its own calendar, Samoa keeps its own way.
